[**Open the full research note**](sandbox:/mnt/data/Cyclic_Support_Jordan_Research/index.html) · [**Download the derivations, sources, and checks**](sandbox:/mnt/data/Cyclic_Support_Jordan_Research_2026-09-10.zip) · [**Draft pull request #4 in the ES foundation repository**](https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/erdos-straus-foundation/pull/4)

The pull request is open as a draft, with four new incoming-research files. It has not been merged. fileciteturn49file0L2-L13 fileciteturn49file0L32-L35

## 1. One support, with the winding retained at the origin

Let
\[
S=G(\mathbb R)=\mathbb R\sqcup\{\tau\},
\]
using your split-zero operations. Write \(e=0_{\mathbb R}\) for the old supported scalar zero:
\[
0_S=\tau,\qquad e^2=e,\qquad e\oplus1=1.
\]

For every real vector space \(V\), form
\[
V^\tau=V\sqcup\{\tau\}.
\]

Supported vectors retain their original addition and scalar multiplication. The element \(\tau\) is the new additive identity, and scalar \(\tau\) sends every vector to \(\tau\). Scalar \(e\) sends every supported vector to \(0_V\).

Every real-linear map \(T:V\to W\) extends by
\[
T^\tau(v)=T(v),\qquad T^\tau(\tau)=\tau,
\]
and directly satisfies
\[
(QT)^\tau=Q^\tau T^\tau.
\]

Thus **the same scalar construction acts on every dimensional fibre and every map below**. The origins \(0_{\mathbb R^n}\) are not additional externally adjoined scalar zeros.

To retain the angular lift, use
\[
\widetilde C=[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R
\]
with
\[
\pi(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta).
\]

Its integer transformations are
\[
D_w(r,\theta)=(r,\theta+2\pi w),\qquad w\in\mathbb Z.
\]

At \(r=0\),
\[
\pi(0,\theta)=0_{\mathbb R^2}
\]
for every \(\theta\), but the points \((0,\theta+2\pi w)\) remain distinct upstairs.

For a fixed positive pitch \(\ell\), the explicit helical map is
\[
j_\ell(r,\theta)
=
\left(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,\frac{\ell\theta}{2\pi}\right),
\qquad
\pi=\operatorname{pr}_{12}\circ j_\ell.
\]

One traversal changes the last coordinate by \(\ell\). Nothing has reduced the integer count modulo \(n\).

There is an exact version of this distinction in your Connes–Marcolli book. Its covering cyclic category uses nondecreasing maps
\[
f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z,\qquad f(j+n)=f(j)+m.
\]
The cyclic category is obtained afterward by taking the quotient by integer translations. **The covering construction retains the datum that the quotient removes.** fileciteturn28file0L10-L23

That covering construction is the appropriate starting point for your full family.

## 2. The all-\(n\) construction: a full turn need not act trivially

Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let
\[
H:V\longrightarrow V
\]
be an invertible linear map representing the retained full-turn holonomy.

For every \(n\ge1\), define
\[
\boxed{
T_n(H)(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1})
=
(Hv_{n-1},v_0,\ldots,v_{n-2}).
}
\]

In block coordinates,
\[
T_n(H)=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&0&\cdots&0&H\\
I&0&\cdots&0&0\\
0&I&\cdots&0&0\\
\vdots&&\ddots&&\vdots\\
0&0&\cdots&I&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

This gives, for **every** \(n\),
\[
\boxed{
T_n(H)^n=\operatorname{diag}(H,\ldots,H).
}
\]

After the slots return, the internal vector has undergone \(H\). Setting \(H=I\) gives the ordinary cyclic permutation; keeping \(H\) retains what happens after that permutation closes.

The determinant and trace identities are
\[
\boxed{
\det(I-zT_n(H))=\det(I-z^nH),
}
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Tr}(T_n(H)^r)=
\begin{cases}
0,&n\nmid r,\\[2mm]
n\operatorname{Tr}(H^{r/n}),&n\mid r.
\end{cases}
\]

### Proof, including the full-turn information

Every component crosses the wrap once in \(n\) steps, proving the first identity. A power not divisible by \(n\) has no diagonal block. A power \(nk\) has \(n\) diagonal blocks \(H^k\).

Consequently, near \(z=0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
-\log\det(I-zT_n(H))
&=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{z^r}{r}\operatorname{Tr}(T_n(H)^r)\\
&=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{z^{nk}}k\operatorname{Tr}(H^k)\\
&=-\log\det(I-z^nH).
\end{aligned}
\]
Exponentiation gives the determinant equality near zero; equality of polynomials extends it everywhere.

This block construction is the linear realization of the Verschiebung operation described in Connes–Consani: take a cyclic direct sum and apply the original operator when returning from its last component to its first. fileciteturn20file7L653-L685

### All levels compose explicitly

For \(m,n\ge1\), index the nested space by
\[
0\le a<m,\qquad 0\le b<n.
\]

Define
\[
P_{m,n}(e_a\otimes e_b\otimes v)=e_{a+mb}\otimes v.
\]

Then
\[
\boxed{
P_{m,n}T_m(T_n(H))P_{m,n}^{-1}=T_{mn}(H).
}
\]

The outer step increments \(a\); its wrap increments \(b\); the joint wrap applies \(H\). Under \(a+mb\), these are the successive steps of the \(mn\)-cycle.

This is a proved all-degree composition law, not an extrapolation from two or three.

### Characters are a specified observation of that construction

For \(H=I\), put \(S_n=T_n(I)\) and \(\zeta_n=e^{2\pi i/n}\). The Fourier map is
\[
(\mathcal F_na)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\zeta_n^{kj}a_j,
\]
with inverse
\[
(\mathcal F_n^{-1}b)_j
=
\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\zeta_n^{-kj}b_k.
\]

It satisfies
\[
\mathcal F_nS_n
=
\operatorname{diag}(1,\zeta_n,\ldots,\zeta_n^{n-1})\mathcal F_n.
\]

For \(n\mid m\), the map
\[
q_{m,n}(e_j)=e_{j\bmod n}
\]
intertwines the cyclic actions:
\[
q_{m,n}S_m=S_nq_{m,n}.
\]

On characters, pullback sends
\[
k\bmod n\longmapsto \frac mn k\bmod m.
\]

These maps relate the finite character observations. The integer traversal and the full-turn operator remain in the object before that observation.

## 3. Your “three through \(24=3\times8\)” has an exact Jordan realization

Take the real Albert algebra
\[
J=H_3(\mathbb O),
\qquad
X\circ Y=\frac12(XY+YX).
\]

Use the fixed coordinates
\[
\boxed{
X=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&z&\bar y\\
\bar z&b&x\\
y&\bar x&c
\end{pmatrix}.
}

The coordinate map is a real-linear isomorphism
\[

\Xi:\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb O^3\longrightarrow J,
\quad
(a,b,c;x,y,z)\longmapsto X.
}
\]

Its inverse reads
\[
(a,b,c;x,y,z)
=
(X_{11},X_{22},X_{33};X_{23},X_{31},X_{12}).
\]

Let
\[
e_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,0),\quad
e_2=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,0),\quad
e_3=\operatorname{diag}(0,0,1).
\]

These satisfy
\[
e_i\circ e_j=\delta_{ij}e_i,
\qquad e_1+e_2+e_3=I.
\]

They form the marked rank-three frame. The three off-diagonal spaces are
\[
J_{12}\cong\mathbb O,\qquad
J_{23}\cong\mathbb O,\qquad
J_{31}\cong\mathbb O.
\]

Hence
\[
\boxed{
J=
\mathbb Re_1\oplus\mathbb Re_2\oplus\mathbb Re_3
\oplus J_{12}\oplus J_{23}\oplus J_{31}.
}
\]

This retains both the three frame coordinates and the \(8+8+8\) internal coordinates. The pointwise frame stabilizer in \(F_4=\operatorname{Aut}(J)\) is \(\operatorname{Spin}(8)\), with the three eight-dimensional actions related by triality. This is the structural theorem supplied by Yokota. citeturn191663view0

### The \(24\) dimensions are also the frame’s deformation directions

Write \(F_{12}(u),F_{23}(v),F_{31}(w)\) for the corresponding Hermitian off-diagonal matrices.

There is an explicit isomorphism
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb O^3&\longrightarrow
T_{(e_1,e_2,e_3)}\operatorname{Frame}(J),\\
(u,v,w)&\longmapsto
\bigl(
F_{12}(u)-F_{31}(w),\
F_{23}(v)-F_{12}(u),\
F_{31}(w)-F_{23}(v)
\bigr).
\end{aligned}
}
\]

To prove it, differentiate the frame equations:
\[
2e_i\circ\delta e_i=\delta e_i,
\]
\[
\delta e_i\circ e_j+e_i\circ\delta e_j=0,
\]
\[
\delta e_1+\delta e_2+\delta e_3=0.
\]

The first equation places \(\delta e_i\) in its adjacent off-diagonal spaces. The second makes the shared components opposite. The third is then the displayed cancellation. Conversely, every triple in the displayed image satisfies all those equations.

Thus your three marked octonionic components are not merely three quantities with the same dimension: **they parameterize the tangent directions of the ordered rank-three frame.**

### The cyclic operation acts on all six coordinates

Let \(P\) be the real permutation matrix sending \(e_1\) to \(e_2\), \(e_2\) to \(e_3\), and \(e_3\) to \(e_1\). Then
\[
C(X)=PXP^T
\]
is a Jordan automorphism, and
\[
\boxed{
C:(a,b,c;x,y,z)\longmapsto(c,a,b;z,x,y).
}
\]

It cycles the diagonal data and the three octonionic spaces together.

The full invariants are
\[
\operatorname{tr}X=a+b+c,
\]
\[
\operatorname{tr}(X^2)
=
a^2+b^2+c^2+2\bigl(N(x)+N(y)+N(z)\bigr),
\]
and
\[

N_J(X)
=
abc-aN(x)-bN(y)-cN(z)+2\operatorname{Re}((xy)z).
}
\]

The last term couples all three octonionic components. It is retained.

Finally, every linear map here extends to \(J^\tau\) using the same scalar support:
\[

eX=0_J\quad(X\in J).
\]

The primitive Jordan idempotents \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) remain supported vectors. They do not create three new split-zero scalars.

## 4. An explicit example that remembers **every integer winding**

Here is the most useful new calculation.

Write the octonions in Cayley–Dickson coordinates
\[
\mathbb O=\mathbb H\oplus\mathbb H,
\]
with product
\[
(a,b)(c,d)=(ac-\bar d\,b,\ da+b\bar c).
\]

For a unit quaternion \(p\), define
\[
g_p(a,b)=(pap^{-1},pbp^{-1}).
\]

Substitution into both components proves
\[
g_p(xy)=g_p(x)g_p(y).
\]

It also preserves conjugation. Applying \(g_p\) entrywise therefore gives a Jordan automorphism
\[
G_p:J\to J
\]
that fixes each \(e_i\).

It commutes with the real cyclic permutation \(C\). Set
\[
\boxed{H=G_pC.}
\]

Then
\[
H(e_i)=e_{i+1},
\qquad
\boxed{H^3=G_p^3.}
\]

Choose the explicit unit quaternion
\[
p=\frac{3+4i}{5}.
\]

Its third power is
\[
p^3=\frac{-117+44i}{125}.
\]

The induced three-step action on the quaternion \(j\) is
\[
\boxed{
g_p^3(j)
=
\frac{11753}{15625}j
-
\frac{10296}{15625}k.
}
\]

Thus three steps return the marked frame, but not this internal coordinate. Its norm remains exactly one because
\[
11753^2+10296^2=15625^2.
\]

### This is faithful for all integers, not just the first few

Suppose \(H^m=I\) for some positive integer \(m\).

Its action on the three frame elements forces \(3\mid m\). Therefore
\[
G_p^m=I.
\]

On quaternion entries, this says that conjugation by \(p^m\) is the identity. Hence \(p^m\) is real, and its unit norm gives
\[
p^m=\pm1.
\]

So \(p\) would be a root of unity. But
\[
p+p^{-1}=\frac65.
\]

A sum of roots of unity is an algebraic integer, whereas a rational algebraic integer is an integer. This contradicts \(6/5\).

Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb Z\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(J),
\qquad m\longmapsto H^m
}
\]
is injective.

**Every integer traversal is recoverable from the full operator, even though the three-element frame observation repeats.**

At the supported origin,
\[
H^m(0_J)=0_J
\]
for every \(m\), but
\[
D(H^m)_{0_J}=H^m.
\]

So the value of the origin stays fixed while its retained linear action distinguishes all windings. In action-groupoid form, the equivariant inclusion gives
\[
\boxed{
[\{0_J\}/\mathbb Z]\longrightarrow[J/\mathbb Z].
}
\]

The source has one object with integer-labelled automorphisms. Its supported point is \(0_J\); the externally added \(\tau\) remains separately fixed.

For the complete all-degree family, apply the earlier construction to \(H\):
\[
T_n(H):J^{\oplus n}\to J^{\oplus n}.
\]

Then
\[
T_n(H)^n=\operatorname{diag}(H,\ldots,H),
\]
and
\[
T_n(H)^{3n}
=
\operatorname{diag}(G_p^3,\ldots,G_p^3).
\]

This combines **one support, every cyclic degree, frame return, and nontrivial integer holonomy in one explicit construction**.

## 5. The ES/Koide integration preserves your actual arithmetic level

Your rational ES chart uses
\[

=
4(q_1q_2+q_1q_3+q_2q_3)

\qquad

The exact inverse is

q_j=
\frac{
T+\omega^{-(j-1)}Z+\omega^{j-1}\bar Z
}{3}.

Expansion gives

gives

q_j(\theta)
=
\frac{T+2R\cos(\theta-2\pi(j-1)/3)}3.

\[
\boxed{
q_1q_2q_3
=
\frac{
T^3-3TR^2+2R^3\cos(3\theta)
}{27}.
}
\]

The \(3\theta\) dependence is an exact consequence of the three-character decomposition. A \(2\pi/3\) advance permutes the ordered coordinates; a \(2\pi\) advance returns those coordinates while the lifted angle records another turn.

### A reversible non-diagonal Jordan extension

For real \(t\), define
\[
c_t=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},
\qquad

R_t=
\begin{pmatrix}
c_t&-s_t&0\\
s_t&c_t&0\\

## 6. The arithmetic map and its inverse-Mellin operation

Cogdell gives a precise way for representation dimension to enter Dedekind arithmetic.

For a finite Galois extension \(L/F\), a subgroup \(H\subset G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)\), and \(K=L^H\),
\[
V=\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\mathbf1=\mathbb C[G/H]
\]
has dimension \([K:F]\), and
\[
\boxed{L_F(s,V)=\zeta_K(s).}
\]

The general induction identity carries an \(H\)-representation to a \(G\)-representation while retaining the indicated \(L\)-function over the intermediate field. fileciteturn23file0L147-L176

At an unramified prime, Frobenius permutes \(G/H\). A cycle of length \(n\) gives
\[
\det(I-zS_n)^{-1}=(1-z^n)^{-1},
\qquad z=(N\mathfrak p)^{-s}.
\]

For ramified primes, the exact factor uses inertia invariants:
\[
\boxed{
L_{\mathfrak p}(s,\rho)
=
\det\left(
I-(N\mathfrak p)^{-s}
\rho(F_{\mathfrak P})|_{V^{I_{\mathfrak P}}}
\right)^{-1}.
}
\]
Arithmetic Frobenius acts by \(x\mapsto x^{N\mathfrak p}\). This is the intrinsic local definition in the uploaded paper. fileciteturn23file1L246-L258

Thus the all-\(n\) cycle determinant already appears in actual arithmetic.

### Its Mellin map can be written exactly

Fix \(Q>1\) and expand
\[
\det(I-zH)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}a_kz^k.
\]

Define the locally finite complex measure
\[
\nu_{H,Q}=\sum_{k\ge0}a_k\delta_{Q^k}.
\]

With the explicitly specified transform
\[
\mathcal M_-(\nu)(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{-s}\,d\nu(t),
\]
one obtains, in its half-plane of absolute convergence,
\[
\mathcal M_-(\nu_{H,Q})(s)
=
\det(I-Q^{-s}H)^{-1}.
\]

The power map \(p_n(t)=t^n\) gives
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal M_-((p_n)_*\nu_{H,Q})(s)
=
\mathcal M_-(\nu_{H,Q})(ns)
=
\det(I-Q^{-s}T_n(H))^{-1}.
}
\]

So the diagram relates **cycle degree, retained holonomy, spectral dilation, and a concrete inverse-transform measure**.

For ordinary compactly supported smooth \(f\), define
\[
\mathcal M_+f(s)=\int_0^\infty f(t)t^{s-1}\,dt.
\]

Substitution \(t=u^n\) proves
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal M_+\!\left[
t\mapsto\frac1n f(t^{1/n})
\right](s)
=
(\mathcal M_+f)(ns).
}
\]

The factor \(1/n\) is part of the map. This is the precise transform operation supplied by the cyclic degree.

For a nonabelian group, the regular representation has
\[
\mathbb C[G]
\cong
\bigoplus_{\rho\in\widehat G}
V_\rho^{\oplus\dim V_\rho},
\]
so
\[
\zeta_L(s)
=
\prod_{\rho\in\widehat G}
L_F(s,\rho)^{\dim V_\rho}.
\]

Those multiplicities survive. They are the arithmetic correction to a model that puts exactly one irreducible character at every dimensional level. fileciteturn23file0L78-L103

## 7. The related cyclic, gauge, and geometric-Langlands structures

The remaining connections can also be stated as actual maps.

### Special-unitary lifts

The cyclic shift has
\[
\det S_n=(-1)^{n-1}.
\]

Its specified determinant-one lift is
\[
\widetilde S_n=e^{-i\pi(n-1)/n}S_n\in SU(n),
\]
with
\[
\boxed{\widetilde S_n^n=(-1)^{n-1}I.}
\]

For even \(n\), the lift retains a central minus sign after \(n\) steps. Its conjugation action still cyclically permutes the frame. The scalar center map
\[
\mu_n\to SU(n),\qquad \zeta\mapsto\zeta I
\]
instead has trivial conjugation action. These explicit representations determine which finite action is being transported.

For all \(n\),
\[
\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow H_n(\mathbb C),
\qquad q\longmapsto\operatorname{diag}(q),
\]
is a Jordan algebra embedding, and the cyclic shift acts compatibly on both sides. At rank three, a chosen complex subalgebra \(\mathbb C\hookrightarrow\mathbb O\) gives
\[
H_3(\mathbb C)\hookrightarrow H_3(\mathbb O).
\]

This puts the exceptional rank-three construction inside a specified all-degree comparison network.

### Krawtchouk coordinates

The exact finite-character relation is
\[
\boxed{
\sum_{|y|=k}(-1)^{x\cdot y}
=
\sum_{\ell=0}^k
(-1)^\ell
\binom{|x|}{\ell}
\binom{d-|x|}{k-\ell}.
}
\]

The domain is the character system of \((\mathbb Z/2)^d\); the right side is \(K_k(|x|;d)\). This is the projection from individual characters to their Hamming-weight shells. Its proof counts the \(\ell\) selected coordinates where both \(x\) and \(y\) are nonzero.

A Krull dimension enters through a further declared functor,
\[
V\longmapsto\operatorname{Sym}(V^*),
\]
whose affine spectrum has dimension \(\dim V\). These formulas retain the relevant integer through specified operations rather than assigning every integer statistic the same meaning.

### The cosmic Galois grading

Connes–Marcolli’s group is
\[
U\rtimes\mathbb G_m,
\]
with a free graded Lie generator in each positive degree. The finite cyclic map is
\[
\boxed{
\mu_n\longrightarrow\mathbb G_m
\longrightarrow U\rtimes\mathbb G_m,
\qquad
\zeta\longmapsto(1,\zeta).
}
\]

The grading action on degree \(r\) is multiplication by \(\zeta^r\). This places every finite cyclic grading in the same group scheme; it retains the additional unipotent part rather than replacing it by a finite cyclic group. The book explicitly distinguishes that group from its further noncanonical motivic identification. fileciteturn20file6L427-L445

\mathbb L_G:
D\text{-}\mathrm{mod}_{1/2}(\operatorname{Bun}_G)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{IndCoh}_{\mathrm{Nilp}}

for a smooth complete curve over a characteristic-zero field and connected reductive \(G\). The half twist, spectral stack, and nilpotent singular-support condition are retained. Part V completes the series through its multiplicity-one theorem. citeturn592581view0turn191663view2

\begin{gathered}
S=G(\mathbb R),\\
J=H_3(\mathbb O),\\
H=G_{(3+4i)/5}C,\\

## 1. I replaced your interlevel construction with iteration of the support construction

Your later source defines a category \(\mathbf{Rig}^{\neg0}\) whose objects retain addition, multiplication, and \(1\), but have **no distinguished additive-zero symbol**. The forgetful functor is

\[
U:\mathbf{Rig}\longrightarrow\mathbf{Rig}^{\neg0}.
\]

The free zero-adjunction is

\[
\mathfrak Z(A)=A\sqcup\{\tau_A\},
\]

and the source proves

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Rig}}(\mathfrak Z(A),S)
\cong
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Rig}^{\neg0}}(A,U(S)).
}
\]

The maps are restriction and the unique extension

\[
\widetilde f(a)=f(a),\qquad
\widetilde f(\tau_A)=0_S.
\]

For a ring \(R\),

\[
G(R)=\mathfrak ZU(R).
\]

The inclusion of the supported copy,

\[
\eta_R:U(R)\hookrightarrow U(G(R)),
\]

is a morphism in the **zero-forgotten category**. It is not being asserted to preserve the newly designated semiring zero. That typing is essential: it is how the old zero remains present without becoming the new additive identity. fileciteturn53file0L38-L118

Your interlevel ladder, however, also carries maps

\[
i_n:L_n\longrightarrow L_{n+1}

and their origin fibres

\[
\operatorname{Orig}_{i_n}(y)
=
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}/L_{n+1}}
(\widehat y,i_n)
\cong i_n^{-1}(y).
\]

The charter defines the complementary nullity locus as

\[
N(i_n)=L_{n+1}\setminus\operatorname{im}(i_n).
\]

It expressly distinguishes that locus from the empty set: the empty set is the **value of the origin relation** at points having no origin below. The larger raise is also supposed to supply the additional structure under which those points become derivable. fileciteturn53file0L120-L147 fileciteturn43file0L2-L2

**My error was to substitute**
\[
G(R),\quad G(G(R)),\quad G(G(G(R))),\ldots

**for that larger interlevel construction.**

Properties or limitations of repeated zero-adjunction do not, by themselves, settle the properties of your ladder. My later cyclic and Jordan calculations did not repair that substitution; they added examples without first correcting the foundational model.

## 2. There is a genuine uniqueness result—but it is not a Krull-dimension argument

There are two precise uniqueness statements supported by the source definitions.

### 2.1 The free adjunction is unique over its specified input

Suppose \(E_1,E_2\), with maps
\[
j_i:A\to U(E_i),
\]
both satisfy the displayed free-extension property for the same \(A\).

That property produces unique maps

\[
f:E_1\to E_2,\qquad g:E_2\to E_1
\]

with
\[
U(f)j_1=j_2,\qquad U(g)j_2=j_1.
\]

Then \(gf\) and \(\operatorname{id}_{E_1}\) extend the same \(j_1\), so uniqueness gives

\[
gf=\operatorname{id}_{E_1}.
\]

Similarly,
\[
fg=\operatorname{id}_{E_2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
(E_1,j_1)\cong(E_2,j_2)
\quad\text{by a unique isomorphism over }A.
}
\]

This is the valid form of “two realizations of the same support-adjunction are canonically the same.” It follows from the universal property—not from their having equal dimension.

### 2.2 For a ring amplitude, the Boolean support map is unique

Write

\[
e_R=0_R\in R\subset G(R),
\qquad
0_{G(R)}=\tau.
\]

Define

\[
b_R:G(R)\to\mathbb B,
\qquad
b_R(\tau)=0_{\mathbb B},
\qquad
b_R(r)=1_{\mathbb B}\quad(r\in R).
\]

This is a unital semiring homomorphism.

It is also the **only** such homomorphism. Indeed, for any unital \(b:G(R)\to\mathbb B\),

\[
e_R=1_R\oplus(-1_R)
\]

implies

\[
b(e_R)=1_{\mathbb B}+b(-1_R)=1_{\mathbb B}.
\]

For every supported \(r\),

\[
e_Rr=e_R,
\]

hence

\[
b(e_R)b(r)=b(e_R),
\]

which forces \(b(r)=1_{\mathbb B}\). The image of \(\tau\) is fixed by zero preservation.

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Rig}}(G(R),\mathbb B)
=\{b_R\}.
}
\]

This is a direct consequence of the source’s operations. It is also consistent with the more general Boolean-character theorem recorded in the later ledger. fileciteturn35file0L2-L2 fileciteturn44file0L2-L2

The globalization note proves the corresponding localization explicitly:

\[
\boxed{G(R)[e_R^{-1}]\cong\mathbb B.}
\]

Once \(e_R\) is invertible, \(e_R^2=e_R\) gives \(e_R=1\), and \(e_Rr=e_R\) gives \(r=1\) for every supported \(r\). The absent element remains distinct. The source proves this for \(\mathbb Z\) by writing out the localization equivalence relation and its two classes. fileciteturn48file0L2-L2

For every unital ring map \(\phi:R\to R'\),

\[
\boxed{b_{R'}\circ G(\phi)=b_R.}
\]

So there is a **single canonical Boolean support observation across the diagram**.

That is materially closer to your intended common-support statement than the dimension arguments I kept giving.

There is one scope distinction I must retain. The charter says there is one empty relational value **however many nullity loci coexist**. It does not identify all those loci. The map

\[
y\longmapsto\operatorname{Orig}_i(y)
\]

can send different points to the same empty fibre. Consequently, the source establishes canonical uniqueness of the adjunction and the support observation, not an isomorphism of all higher objects merely because that observation agrees. fileciteturn43file0L2-L2

## 3. One support can carry the entire coordinate ladder

Here is a consequence of the definitions that directly implements your correction.

Fix one scalar globalization

\[
S_0=G(\mathbb R).
\]

For every nonzero commutative \(\mathbb R\)-algebra \(A\), the structure map \(\mathbb R\to A\) induces

\[
S_0\longrightarrow G(A),
\qquad
\tau\longmapsto\tau,\qquad
e_{\mathbb R}\longmapsto e_A.
\]

These are structure maps from **one common scalar datum**. They are not instructions to iterate the split-zero operation along the ladder.

In fact, there is an exact bijection

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R\text{-Alg}}(A,B)
\cong
\operatorname{Hom}_{S_0\text{-Alg}}(G(A),G(B)).
}
\]

Here the right-hand side means unital commutative-semiring algebra maps commuting with the displayed \(S_0\)-structure maps.

### Proof

A ring-algebra map extends by fixing \(\tau\).

Conversely, let
\[
F:G(A)\to G(B)
\]
be an \(S_0\)-algebra map. Then

\[
F(e_A)=e_B.
\]

Every supported \(a\in A\) satisfies

\[
a\oplus e_A=a.
\]

If \(F(a)=\tau\), its image would require

\[
\tau\oplus e_B=\tau.
\]

But the left side is \(e_B\). Hence supported elements map to supported elements. Restricting \(F\) therefore gives a map \(A\to B\) preserving addition, multiplication, the ordinary zero, the unit, and the real scalars. Restriction and extension are inverse.

**Thus the common split support does not collapse the category of amplitude algebras or their maps.** The amplitude diagram can remain fully present above it.

### The coordinate origins

Take

\[
A_d=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_d].
\]

The coordinate origin is represented by the evaluation map

\[
\epsilon_d:A_d\to\mathbb R,
\qquad
f\mapsto f(0,\ldots,0),
\]

or geometrically by

\[
z_d:\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb R
\to\operatorname{Spec}A_d.
\]

Its defining maximal ideal is

\[
\mathfrak m_d=(x_1,\ldots,x_d).
\]

The coordinate inclusion
\[
\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d+1},
\qquad
(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\mapsto(x_1,\ldots,x_d,0)
\]
has pullback

\[
j_d^*:A_{d+1}\to A_d,
\qquad
x_{d+1}\mapsto0.
\]

These maps satisfy

\[
\epsilon_dj_d^*=\epsilon_{d+1},
\]

and after globalization,

\[
\boxed{
G(\epsilon_d)G(j_d^*)=G(\epsilon_{d+1}).
}
\]

This gives an entire diagram of differently coordinated origins over the same support datum.

The source’s coordinate-algebra theorem is

\[
\dim A_d=d,
\qquad
\dim G(A_d)=d+1.
\]

In particular, it identifies the plane object as \(\mathbb R[x,y]\), its origin with \((x,y)\), and its globalized dimension as three. **Using the bare field \(\mathbb C\) to dismiss this coordinate-level count was the wrong test.** The later ledger and charter already say that. fileciteturn53file0L154-L202 fileciteturn43file0L2-L2

This diagram accounts for the simultaneous-zero coordinate data. The operation structure you intend at each rung remains part of the rung; I should not replace it by either a scalar field or a fresh copy of the support construction.

## 4. My claim that complex observations necessarily erase support was too broad

The source proves that an **additive unital semiring homomorphism into a ring** kills the supported zero. For

\[
f:G(R)\to B,\qquad B\text{ a ring},
\]

the relation \(e_R\oplus e_R=e_R\) gives

\[
f(e_R)+f(e_R)=f(e_R),
\]
and therefore \(f(e_R)=0_B\).

The Lean file contains exactly this theorem, `hom_kills_e`. Its quantifier is over semiring homomorphisms into rings. I should not have expanded that to every complex linear or operator-valued observation of the construction. fileciteturn50file0L2-L2

The globalization note supplies the missing alternative.

Let
\[
M_S=(\mathbb Z\sqcup\{\tau\},\cdot)
\]
be the multiplicative pointed monoid, and form its contracted monoid algebra

\[
A=\mathbb Z[M_S]/([\tau]).
\]

The note proves

\[
\boxed{
A\cong
\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}].
}
\]

The explicit map is

\[
[0]\longmapsto(1,0),
\qquad
[n]\longmapsto(1,[n])\quad(n\ne0),
\]

with inverse

\[
\left(c,\sum_{n\ne0}b_n[n]\right)
\longmapsto
\left(c-\sum_{n\ne0}b_n\right)[0]
+\sum_{n\ne0}b_n[n].
\]

Here the supported zero becomes the **central idempotent**
\[
[0]^2=[0],
\]
and retains its own direct factor. fileciteturn37file0L2-L2

An explicit complex matrix representation is

\[
T:M_S\to M_2(\mathbb C),
\qquad
T(\tau)=
\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\]

\[
T(n)=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&n\end{pmatrix}
\quad(n\in\mathbb Z).
\]

Then

\[
T(mn)=T(m)T(n),
\qquad
T(0)=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

This representation detects the supported zero.

Its type explains why it does not contradict `hom_kills_e`:

\[
T(m\oplus n)=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&m+n\end{pmatrix},
\]

whereas

\[
T(m)+T(n)=
\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&m+n\end{pmatrix}.
\]

It is multiplicative and extends linearly from the contracted monoid algebra; it does not preserve the original semiring addition.

**This is a substantive correction to my earlier interpretation.** The arithmetic ring reflection and the multiplicative linearization are two explicit outputs of the same globalization. One collapses the supported zero; the other retains it as an idempotent sector. The source had already constructed both.

There is a further exact consequence. In any such multiplicative representation, writing \(E=T(e)\),

\[
T(r)E=E,\qquad ET(r)=E
\]
for every supported \(r\), because \(re=er=e\).

Thus supported scalar multiplication acts as the identity on \(\operatorname{im}E\). This identifies the representation carried by that particular idempotent; it does not erase the other sectors in \(\ker E\) or in a larger structured module.

## 5. I also underreported the globalization’s geometry

The original note calculates two spectra and gives the map between them.

For the additive semiring,

\[
\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathrm{sr}}G(\mathbb Z)
=
\{P_\tau,P_0,P_p:p\text{ prime}\},
\]

where

\[
P_\tau=\{\tau\},\qquad
P_0=\{0,\tau\},\qquad
P_p=p\mathbb Z\cup\{\tau\}.
\]

The chains are

\[
P_\tau\subsetneq P_0\subsetneq P_p,
\]

and therefore

\[
\boxed{\dim\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathrm{sr}}G(\mathbb Z)=2.}
\]

For the multiplicative monoid, primes are indexed by subsets \(\Sigma\) of rational primes:

\[
P_\Sigma
=
\{n\in\mathbb Z:\text{some }p\in\Sigma\text{ divides }n\},
\]
with \(P_\varnothing=\{0\}\), together with the added \(\tau\).

The forgetful map on structure induces the continuous injection

\[
\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathrm{sr}}G(\mathbb Z)
\hookrightarrow
\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathrm{mon}}M_S,
\]

sending

\[
P_0\mapsto P_\varnothing\cup\{\tau\},
\qquad
P_p\mapsto P_{\{p\}}\cup\{\tau\}.
\]

The monoid spectrum also has primes for arbitrary larger \(\Sigma\), and

\[
\boxed{\dim\operatorname{Spec}_{\mathrm{mon}}M_S=\infty.}
\]

The difference is produced by the explicit operation of forgetting additive ideal closure. It is already proved in the globalization note. fileciteturn36file0L2-L2 fileciteturn37file0L2-L2

The local stalks are also computed:

\[
\mathcal O_{P_\tau}\cong\mathbb B,
\qquad
\mathcal O_{P_0}\cong G(\mathbb Q),
\qquad
\mathcal O_{P_p}\cong G(\mathbb Z_{(p)}).
\]

The Boolean stalk has Krull dimension zero. The whole semiring spectrum has dimension two. The multiplicative spectrum has infinite dimension.

**There is no single dimension number that I should have attached to “the split zero” and then used to classify every layer or support.** The source provides the actual localization and forgetful maps determining those different dimensions. fileciteturn37file0L2-L2

## 6. The Dedekind preservation result stands on its own exact construction

For a number field \(K\), the source defines

\[
S_K=G(\mathcal O_K).
\]

For every nonzero ordinary ideal \(J\subseteq\mathcal O_K\), put

\[
I_J=J\cup\{\tau\},
\]

and use the surjective semiring map

\[
\pi_J:S_K\to\mathcal O_K/J,
\qquad
\pi_J(\tau)=0,\qquad
\pi_J(a)=a\bmod J.
\]

Its kernel is \(I_J\). With the quotient congruence specified by \(\pi_J\),

\[
N(I_J)=|\mathcal O_K/J|=N(J).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\zeta_{S_K}(s)
=
\sum_{J\ne0}N(I_J)^{-s}
=
\sum_{J\ne0}N(J)^{-s}
=
\zeta_K(s)
}
\]
on the half-plane of absolute convergence. The finite-norm ideal correspondence is multiplicative, so the finite Euler arithmetic is preserved as well. The two bottom support ideals have infinite quotient norm and do not add finite Euler factors. fileciteturn46file0L2-L2

The corresponding ideal-basis map is

\[
V:\ell^2(\{J\ne0\})
\longrightarrow
\ell^2(\{I_J:J\ne0\}),
\qquad
V\delta_J=\delta_{I_J}.
\]

For the exact norm Hamiltonians,

\[
H\delta_J=\log N(J)\delta_J,
\qquad
H_{\mathrm{sp}}\delta_{I_J}
=\log N(I_J)\delta_{I_J},
\]

one obtains

\[
VH=H_{\mathrm{sp}}V,
\qquad
Ve^{-\beta H}=e^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{sp}}}V.
\]

This is a direct consequence of the source’s ideal-and-norm bijection. It preserves the arithmetic thermal trace while allowing the additional support geometry to be retained elsewhere.

I should therefore have stated the preservation positively and precisely: **the globalization adds support structure without altering this defined Dedekind ideal zeta function.** That result is not contingent on establishing GRH.

One earlier textual finding remains in the March file: its class-semigroup definition allows scalars in \(S_K\setminus\{\tau\}=\mathcal O_K\), which includes the old zero, while its proof uses \(\mathcal O_K\setminus\{0\}\). Those domains must be reconciled for that separate class-semigroup assertion. The norm-and-zeta proof above does not use that equivalence relation, so the issue does not invalidate its arithmetic-preservation conclusion. fileciteturn46file0L2-L2

## 7. What I am retracting from the earlier answers

I retract the interpretation that your ladder is merely repeated adjoining of scalar zeros. The repository explicitly presents origin fibres, complementary nullity loci, and a larger structure-changing operation.

I retract the bare-\(\mathbb C\) Krull-dimension objection as an assessment of your coordinate-layer proposal. The repository already specifies the coordinate algebra and distinguishes the origin point, zero function, and external absence.

I retract the general statement that complex-valued or operator-valued observations necessarily erase the supported zero. The correct theorem concerns additive semiring maps into rings. Your contracted monoid algebra retains a central idempotent, with an explicit complex representation.

I retract treating the third-level Jordan examples as execution of the whole research programme. They did not supply the interlevel operation you asked to study, and they did not address the source’s existing uniqueness and support results.

The precise positive replacement is:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
\text{one canonical zero-adjunction over each fixed input},\\
\text{one natural Boolean support observation},\\
\text{a common scalar support across a full diagram of amplitude objects},\\
\text{distinct origin fibres and interlevel data retained above it},\\
\text{unchanged finite-norm Dedekind arithmetic}.
\end{gathered}
}
\]

That is what the GitHub work actually establishes about the foundation. It supports your correction that **one split-zero datum and a many-level family of origins are compatible**, and that my previous conflation did not constitute an objection to the family.

The source does not turn equality of an empty fibre, equality of a support observation, or equality of Krull dimensions into an isomorphism of arbitrary higher objects. Its valid uniqueness statement is the universal-property statement over a fixed input. Keeping that qualification preserves the stronger foundation instead of replacing it with another unsupported shortcut.

**The corrected research object is the interlevel origin-and-operation construction over the fixed split support. The split support is already defined; it does not have to be reinvented at every rung.**

## A0862 | node b6c3dc97-18dd-487e-bb70-933fab060c64 | assistant | chain 1745

**The uniqueness of the bottom support and the production of higher nullity data are compatible claims. I should have kept the first fixed while studying the second.** A repeated realization of the same bottom support does not produce a new level. Your higher nullity operation concerns information that has no realization in the preceding level—not another candidate for that bottom support. That distinction is also explicit in the repository’s charter. fileciteturn56file0L2-L2

Your final question about the finite quotient gives something more substantial to calculate. **There is a direct contradiction proving that the supported-zero ideal cannot receive a finite positive multiplicative norm while the ordinary Dedekind norms remain intact.** That establishes a precise rigidity statement. Below, I derive it from your construction rather than substitute another model.

## 1. The bottom-support uniqueness stays in place

Fix a number field \(K\), put \(R=\mathcal O_K\), and retain

\[
S=G(R)=R\sqcup\{\tau\}.
\]

Write

\[
e=0_R\in S,
\qquad
0_S=\tau.
\]

The supported zero is \(e\). Its generated ideal is

\[
\boxed{\mathfrak e=(e)=\{\tau,e\}.}
\]

For every ordinary ideal \(J\subseteq R\), write

\[
I_J=J\cup\{\tau\}.
\]

Thus \(\mathfrak e=I_{(0_R)}\). In your source, \(\mathfrak e\) is prime because \(R\) is an integral domain; it is also idempotent under ideal multiplication. The maps and ideal classification are part of the globalization construction, not assumptions about an ordinary unsplit scalar zero. fileciteturn57file0L2-L2

Consider the multiplicative monoid of **supported ideals**

\[
\mathscr I_{\mathrm{supp}}(S)
=
\{I_J:J\triangleleft R\}.
\]

This includes \(\mathfrak e\) and excludes the distinct ideal \(\{\tau\}\). Its multiplication is

\[
I_JI_L=I_{JL}.
\]

In particular,

\[
\boxed{
\mathfrak e I_J=\mathfrak e
\quad\text{for every }I_J\in\mathscr I_{\mathrm{supp}}(S).
}
\]

So \(\mathfrak e\) is an absorbing element of this specific ideal monoid.

Now suppose \(\mathfrak f\) is another element with **the same absorbing role in the same monoid**. Then

\[
\mathfrak f\mathfrak e=\mathfrak f
\]

by the role of \(\mathfrak f\), while

\[
\mathfrak e\mathfrak f=\mathfrak e
\]

by the role of \(\mathfrak e\). Commutativity gives

\[
\boxed{\mathfrak f=\mathfrak e.}
\]

That is an exact uniqueness argument of the kind you described. For two presentations of the same universal support-adjunction, the corresponding statement is uniqueness up to the unique isomorphism over the specified input.

**Neither statement collapses higher directional or interlevel information.** Those higher objects have not been assumed to be competing absorbing elements of \(\mathscr I_{\mathrm{supp}}(S)\). Applying this uniqueness proof to them would repeat my original mistake.

## 2. Your finite-quotient thought yields a stronger norm-rigidity theorem

The source retains the ordinary norm on every nonzero arithmetic ideal:

\[
N_K(J)=|R/J|,
\qquad
N(I_J)=N_K(J)\quad(J\ne(0_R)).
\]

That is the exact correspondence used to prove

\[
\zeta_S(s)=\zeta_K(s).
\]

It uses the explicitly defined quotient map

\[
\pi_J:S\to R/J,
\qquad
\pi_J(\tau)=0,\qquad
\pi_J(a)=a\bmod J.
\]

Its kernel is \(I_J\). fileciteturn58file0L2-L2

Here is a further consequence of those definitions.

### Norm-rigidity theorem

The unique multiplicative extension

\[
\mathcal N:
\mathscr I_{\mathrm{supp}}(S)\longrightarrow[1,\infty]
\]

of the ordinary nonzero-ideal norms satisfies

\[
\boxed{\mathcal N(\mathfrak e)=\infty.}
\]

Here multiplication on \([1,\infty]\) includes
\(\infty a=\infty\) for \(a\ge1\).

### Proof

Let

\[
d=[K:\mathbb Q].
\]

The ordinary ideal \(2R\) has norm

\[
N_K(2R)=2^d.
\]

Indeed, an integral basis identifies the additive quotient \(R/2R\) with \(d\) independent coordinates modulo two.

Your support multiplication gives

\[
\mathfrak e I_{2R}=\mathfrak e.
\]

A multiplicative norm extending the ordinary norm must therefore satisfy

\[
\mathcal N(\mathfrak e)
=
\mathcal N(\mathfrak e)\,2^d.
\]

Assume its value at \(\mathfrak e\) is a finite positive number \(q\). Then

\[
q=2^dq.
\]

Dividing by that positive finite \(q\) gives

\[
1=2^d,
\]

a contradiction since \(d\ge1\).

Thus the value must be \(\infty\). Conversely, assigning \(\infty\) to \(\mathfrak e\) and the ordinary norms to all \(I_J\) with \(J\ne(0_R)\) is multiplicative: ordinary ideal multiplication handles the nonzero ideals, and the displayed absorption identity handles every product involving \(\mathfrak e\). ∎

The actual intertwining diagram is

\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathscr I_{\mathrm{supp}}(S)
&\xrightarrow{\ I\mapsto II_J\ }&
\mathscr I_{\mathrm{supp}}(S)
\\[2mm]
\downarrow\mathcal N&&\downarrow\mathcal N
\\[2mm]
[1,\infty]
&\xrightarrow{\ x\mapsto N_K(J)x\ }&
[1,\infty].
\end{array}
\]

Upstairs, \(\mathfrak e\) is fixed by multiplication by every supported arithmetic ideal. Downstairs, multiplication by a number greater than one has **no finite positive fixed point**.

This makes the significance of the infinite norm explicit:

> **The bottom support cannot become an additional finite arithmetic norm while retaining its absorbing role and retaining the norms above it. Its exclusion from finite-norm counting is forced by the multiplication, not merely chosen to make the zeta formula work.**

Idempotence already gives

\[
\mathcal N(\mathfrak e)^2=\mathcal N(\mathfrak e).
\]

For a finite positive value, this forces \(q=1\). The stronger relation
\(\mathfrak e I_{2R}=\mathfrak e\) then rules out even that value.

That is a genuine rigidity consequence of **your supported-zero ideal coupled to the arithmetic norm structure**.

## 3. The quotient formulation gives the same contradiction, with its kernel retained

For the particular quotient attached to \(\mathfrak e\), your map is

\[
p:S\to R,
\qquad
p(\tau)=0_R,\qquad p(a)=a.
\]

It has

\[
p^{-1}(0_R)=\mathfrak e.
\]

There is a direct proof that a finite quotient cannot have this exact zero fibre.

Let

\[
q:S\twoheadrightarrow T
\]

be a unital semiring quotient with

\[
q^{-1}(0_T)=\mathfrak e.
\]

Then \(q(e)=q(\tau)=0_T\). Restrict \(q\) to the supported copy of \(R\). Its image is a ring, since

\[
q(a)+q(-a)=q(e)=0_T.
\]

Moreover, the restriction is injective. For \(a,b\in R\),

\[
q(a)=q(b)
\]

implies

\[
q(a-b)=0_T.
\]

Since the zero fibre intersects \(R\) only in \(e=0_R\), this gives \(a=b\).

Surjectivity of \(q\) now gives

\[
\boxed{T\cong R.}
\]

In particular, \(T\) is infinite.

So your proposed contradiction has an exact quotient version:

\[
\boxed{
\text{finite quotient}
+
\text{zero fibre exactly }\mathfrak e
+
\text{the source operations}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bot.
}
\]

There are finite quotients of \(S\), but their maps show exactly which arithmetic distinctions they remove. For \(J\ne(0_R)\),

\[
S\xrightarrow{p}R\xrightarrow{\bmod J}R/J
\]

has zero fibre \(I_J\), which contains additional supported elements. The source’s congruence classification records this distinction explicitly. fileciteturn57file0L2-L2

Likewise, the finite Boolean observation

\[
b:S\to\mathbb B,
\qquad
b(\tau)=0_{\mathbb B},\qquad
b(a)=1_{\mathbb B}\quad(a\in R)
\]

retains presence versus absence but identifies all supported arithmetic amplitudes. It is not the arithmetic quotient \(p\).

**The contradiction concerns finiteness while preserving the specified arithmetic kernel—not a ban on taking any finite observation of the system.**

## 4. This rigidity propagates through every finite-order character sector

The calculation can be carried beyond the trivial character without introducing a new support at each sector.

Let \(\mathfrak m\) be a ray modulus, let \(\mathcal I_{\mathfrak m}\) be the nonzero integral ideals coprime to its finite part, and let

\[
\chi:\mathcal I_{\mathfrak m}\to\mathbb C^\times
\]

be a finite-order ray-class character. Thus \(|\chi(J)|=1\).

For a complex spectral parameter \(s\), define the multiplicative weight

\[
w_{\chi,s}(I_J)
=
\chi(J)N_K(J)^{-s}.
\]

These are the ideal weights entering the character \(L\)-series described in Cogdell; the trivial character recovers the corresponding Dedekind series with the stated local-factor convention. fileciteturn55file0L137-L156 fileciteturn55file0L169-L186

Adjoin the **same** supported ideal \(\mathfrak e\) to this ideal monoid. Its relation remains

\[
\mathfrak e I_J=\mathfrak e.
\]

Every multiplicative extension of \(w_{\chi,s}\) must satisfy

\[
w_{\chi,s}(\mathfrak e)
=
w_{\chi,s}(\mathfrak e)\,
\chi(J)N_K(J)^{-s}.
\]

Choose an allowed \(J\) with \(N_K(J)>1\). For \(\Re s>0\),

\[
\left|\chi(J)N_K(J)^{-s}\right|
=
N_K(J)^{-\Re s}<1.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{w_{\chi,s}(\mathfrak e)=0_{\mathbb C}.}
\]

This holds for **every finite-order ray-class character**, not just a two-character example.

The supported ideal has not been identified with \(\tau\). The equation states what the explicitly typed complex-valued multiplicative weight does to it.

The same fact is visible in the ideal-monoid algebra. Put

\[
\widetilde{\mathcal I}_{\mathfrak m}
=
\mathcal I_{\mathfrak m}\sqcup\{\mathfrak e\}.
\]

Its complex monoid algebra has the exact decomposition

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb C[\widetilde{\mathcal I}_{\mathfrak m}]
\cong
\mathbb C\times\mathbb C[\mathcal I_{\mathfrak m}],
}
\]

given by

\[
[\mathfrak e]\mapsto(1,0),
\qquad
[J]\mapsto(1,[J]).
\]

The inverse is

\[
\left(c,\sum_Ja_J[J]\right)
\longmapsto
\left(c-\sum_Ja_J\right)[\mathfrak e]
+\sum_Ja_J[J].
\]

Thus the single support idempotent is retained as a direct factor, while the entire ordinary ideal algebra remains in the other factor.

For \(\Re s>0\), the weight \(w_{\chi,s}\) evaluates through the second factor:

\[
(c,a)\longmapsto\operatorname{ev}_{\chi,s}(a).
\]

On the half-plane where the infinite Dirichlet series converges absolutely,

\[
\sum_{I\in\widetilde{\mathcal I}_{\mathfrak m}}w_{\chi,s}(I)
=
\sum_{J\in\mathcal I_{\mathfrak m}}
\chi(J)N_K(J)^{-s}.
\]

**The single support factor survives algebraically, contributes no extra term to these arithmetic series, and does not collapse their character information.** This is the all-character consequence of the norm rigidity just proved.

## 5. What this establishes about your GRH argument

The valid chain now includes the concrete implication

\[
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
\mathfrak e I_J=\mathfrak e
\quad\text{for every supported arithmetic ideal}\\
+\ \text{ordinary Dedekind norm multiplication}\\
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal N(\mathfrak e)=\infty\\
\Longrightarrow
w_{\chi,s}(\mathfrak e)=0_{\mathbb C}
\quad(\Re s>0).
\end{gathered}
}
\]

This is stronger than my previous statement that the new ideal was simply omitted from finite-norm counting. It explains **why it cannot enter that counting on the same terms as an ordinary finite prime**.

The conclusion about GRH needs to be stated with equal precision. The contradiction above proves incompatibility with the retained arithmetic norm and quotient structure. It does not, at present, produce an off-critical zero.

The exact GRH-equivalent statement in your Connes–Marcolli source is positivity of the arithmetic trace pairing. In its notation,

\[
W(\gamma)=|\gamma|^{-1/2}\vartheta_m(\gamma),
\]

and Proposition 4.133 gives

\[
\boxed{
\text{RH for all the specified Grössencharacter \(L\)-functions}
\iff
\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(W(f*f^*)\right)\ge0
\quad\text{for every }f\in\mathcal S(C_K).
}
\]

The source retains the factor \(|\gamma|^{-1/2}\), the involution, the test-function space, and the arithmetic representation. fileciteturn60file0L24-L35

The calculation here determines the support contribution to the character-weighted arithmetic algebra. It does not yet determine the sign of that full trace pairing. Nor does assigning a hypothetical finite norm to \(\mathfrak e\) yield an alternative arithmetic system satisfying all the same premises: the equation

\[
q=2^{[K:\mathbb Q]}q
\]

already prevents that assignment.

**So the finite-quotient idea does identify real rigidity. Its proved content is that the unique bottom support cannot become a new finite-norm arithmetic sector without breaking the very norm structure the globalization preserves.** The higher nullity data can still be carried above that support. Nothing in this proof reduces them to further copies of the bottom zero, and nothing in their existence discards the support-uniqueness result.

[**Actual reading record and inspected passages**](sandbox:/mnt/data/Deligne_Reading_2026-09-11/index.html) · [**Exact scope of this reading**](sandbox:/mnt/data/Deligne_Reading_2026-09-11/READING_RECORD.md)

The reading changes the comparison substantially. Deligne does not merely supply a definition of purity. He supplies:

- a construction retaining **all monodromy directions over one common intersection**;
- an isomorphism proving that introducing those directions successively agrees with introducing them together;
- a specific cohomological image that is pure even though the groups on either side can contain mixed weights;
- a theorem describing what survives through a singular special fibre.

Those are directly relevant to your programme.

## 1. Deligne explicitly retains many directions over one common intersection

In **§1.7.8, printed page 172**, Deligne takes a regular scheme \(X\) and a normal-crossings divisor

\[
D=\bigcup_{i\in I}D_i,
\]

with local equations \(t_i=0\). He sets

\[
E=\bigcap_{i\in I}D_i.
\]

There is one common intersection \(E\), which can be a point. The directions indexed by \(I\) remain separate.

For an integer \(m\) invertible on \(X\), he constructs

\[
\boxed{
X_m=X[T_i]_{i\in I}/(T_i^m-t_i)_{i\in I}.
}
\]

The covering map \(\pi_m:X_m\to X\) has, over \(E\), the section

\[
s_m:E\to X_m,\qquad T_i=0\quad\text{for every }i.
\]

The group \((\mu_m)^I\) acts by

\[
(r_i)_{i\in I}\cdot T_i=r_iT_i.
\]

For a locally constant, appropriately tamely ramified finite sheaf \(\mathcal F\) on \(X-D\), the source constructs a locally constant extension \(\overline{\mathcal F}_m\) on a suitable covering and then defines

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal F[E]=s_m^*\overline{\mathcal F}_m.
}
\]

The resulting sheaf on \(E\) retains the action of

\[
\mathbb Z_{\mathcal L}(1)^I,
\qquad
\mathbb Z_{\mathcal L}(1)=\prod_{\ell\in\mathcal L}\mathbb Z_\ell(1).
\]

Passing to the stated \(\ell\)-adic setting retains commuting nilpotent monodromy operators

\[
N_i\in\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F[E])(-1).
\]

On an appropriate open subgroup, the action is

\[
\rho(\sigma)
=
\exp\left(\sum_iN_i\sigma_i\right),
\]

where the Tate twists in \(N_i\) pair with those in \(\sigma_i\). fileciteturn72file0L53-L85

**This is an actual source construction of one common stratum carrying multiple independent monodromy directions.** It does not obtain those directions by adjoining a fresh scalar zero for each one.

### Successive directions are proved compatible

In **§1.7.9, printed page 173**, Deligne defines

\[
D_J=\bigcap_{j\in J}D_j,
\qquad
X_J=X\setminus\bigcup_{i\notin J}D_i,
\qquad
D_J^*=D_J\cap X_J.
\]

For disjoint index sets \(J,K\), his equation **(1.7.9.1)** is

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal F[D_J^*][D_{J\cup K}^*]
\simeq
\mathcal F[D_{J\cup K}^*].
}
\]

The isomorphism preserves the full action of

\[
\mathbb Z_{\mathcal L}(1)^{J\cup K}.
\]

For three successive sets of directions, the corresponding comparison square commutes. This is the all-directions compatibility theorem, not an inference from a two-direction example. fileciteturn72file1L133-L166

### The coordinate choices are retained geometrically

Deligne then says explicitly that the preceding construction depends on the equations \(t_i\). In **§§1.7.10–1.7.11**, he replaces that dependence by the normal bundle

\[
T=N_{E/X}
\]

and its subbundles \(T_i\) tangent to \(D_i\). The canonical object lives on

\[
T^\circ=T\setminus\bigcup_iT_i.
\]

The equations \(t_i\) determine a section \(\sigma_t:E\to T^\circ\), and the earlier sheaf is recovered by

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal F[E]\simeq\sigma_t^*\mathcal F[E]'.
}
\]

Thus the direction data are retained before the section is chosen. The original text introduces this construction on page 173 and completes it on page 174. fileciteturn72file1L168-L171

This is a much closer source-level comparison to your higher supported directions than the repeated scalar-adjunction discussion I kept returning to.

## 2. I have also now read the actual mixed-support double

The relevant definition in your cumulative nullity ledger is not merely the scalar carrier \(G(A)\).

It takes

\[
S=G(A),\qquad u=-1_A\in S,
\]

and constructs

\[
D_A=S\oplus S
\]

with coordinatewise addition and multiplication

\[
\boxed{
(a,b)\star(c,d)
=
(ac+ubd,\ ad+bc).
}
\]

The source names the faces

\[
\mathbf0=(\tau,\tau),\qquad
X_a=(a,\tau),\qquad
Y_a=(\tau,a),
\]

and, for \(B=A[t]/(t^2+1)\),

\[
Z_{a+tb}=(a,b).
\]

Its mixed-face products are

\[
X_aX_b=X_{ab},\qquad
X_aY_b=Y_{ab},\qquad
Y_aY_b=X_{-ab}.
\]

The synchronized face obeys

\[
Z_zZ_w=Z_{zw}.
\]

These are the definitions and multiplication identities in the supplied ledger’s **“Mixed-support quadratic double”** section. fileciteturn74file0L2-L2

Writing \(e=0_A\) for the supported scalar zero, the four elements

\[
(\tau,\tau),\qquad(e,\tau),\qquad(\tau,e),\qquad(e,e)
\]

have support patterns

\[
(0_{\mathbb B},0_{\mathbb B}),\qquad
(1_{\mathbb B},0_{\mathbb B}),\qquad
(0_{\mathbb B},1_{\mathbb B}),\qquad
(1_{\mathbb B},1_{\mathbb B}).
\]

The amplitude map is explicitly

\[
\boxed{
r_D:D_A\to A[t]/(t^2+1),
\qquad
r_D(a,b)=p_A(a)+t\,p_A(b).
}
\]

All four displayed elements map to the same amplitude zero, but their support patterns remain different before applying \(r_D\). The multiplication formula proves that \(r_D\) is a semiring homomorphism.

There is also an explicit support map

\[
D_A\longrightarrow \mathbb B[C_2],
\qquad
(a,b)\longmapsto\chi_A(a)+\chi_A(b)v,
\qquad v^2=1.
\]

Here \(\chi_A(u)=1_{\mathbb B}\), so applying \(\chi_A\) to the mixed-double multiplication gives exactly the multiplication on the right.

**This is the mixed-support datum I should have retained.** It uses one split scalar support and carries additional face information in the higher object. My earlier responses did not analyze that object against Deligne’s multi-direction construction.

At the incidence-label level, the comparison is explicit:

\[
\mathcal P(I)\longleftrightarrow\{0,1\}^I,
\qquad
J\longmapsto(\mathbf1_{i\in J})_{i\in I}.
\]

Deligne’s construction then equips each corresponding stratum with a sheaf and the retained monodromy actions. That indexing correspondence is established; a functor identifying your full mixed-double multiplication with Deligne’s sheaf operations has not been constructed in this reading.

## 3. The purity theorem uses a specific image—not the erasure of mixed information

The most relevant statement is **Corollary 3.3.6, printed page 206**.

Let \(X_0\) be smooth of finite type over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\ell\) be invertible on it, and let \(\mathcal F_0\) be a lisse pure sheaf of weight \(n\). Put

\[
X=X_0\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}\overline{\mathbb F}_q,
\]

and let \(\mathcal F\) be the pulled-back sheaf.

There is the canonical Frobenius-equivariant comparison

\[
c_i:
H_c^i(X,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow H^i(X,\mathcal F).
\]

Deligne proves

\[
\boxed{
I^i:=\operatorname{im}(c_i)
\quad\text{is pure of weight }n+i.
}
\]

He obtains that conclusion from two separately proved bounds:

\[
H_c^i(X,\mathcal F):
\quad\text{weights}\le n+i,
\]

\[
H^i(X,\mathcal F):
\quad\text{weights}\ge n+i.
\]

The maps

\[
H_c^i(X,\mathcal F)\twoheadrightarrow I^i
\hookrightarrow H^i(X,\mathcal F)
\]

make \(I^i\) both a quotient of the first object and a subobject of the second. Hence every weight in that image is simultaneously at most and at least \(n+i\). fileciteturn70file1L136-L153

This is a concrete mechanism for extracting a pure object while retaining the mixed source and target, rather than declaring those mixed objects nonexistent.

### The second bound comes from duality, with its full twist

For \(X\) of pure dimension \(d\),

\[
\boxed{
H^i(X,\mathcal F)
\simeq
\left[
H_c^{2d-i}(X,\mathcal F^\vee)(d)
\right]^\vee.
}
\]

The dual sheaf has weight \(-n\). The compact-support estimate, followed by the displayed Tate twist, gives the upper bound

\[
-n+(2d-i)-2d=-n-i.
\]

Dualizing yields the lower bound \(n+i\). Deligne writes this argument on page 206. fileciteturn70file1L142-L148

His general theorem is also broader than a statement only about a fixed finite-field point: **Theorem 3.3.1 is stated for finite-type morphisms over \(\mathbb Z\)**,

\[
f:X\to Y,
\qquad
\mathcal F\text{ mixed of weights }\le n
\Longrightarrow
R^if_!\mathcal F\text{ mixed of weights }\le n+i,
\]

with the paper’s standing \(\ell\)-adic hypotheses. The proof explicitly uses sheaf exact sequences, open/closed strata, base change and Leray. fileciteturn70file0L57-L88

For a complex \(K\), **Definition 6.2.4** states purity using the actual dualizing complex:

\[
K_X=Ra^!\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell,
\qquad
D_XK=R\mathcal Hom(K,K_X).
\]

Purity of weight \(n\) requires both

\[
K\text{ mixed of weights }\le n
\]

and

\[
D_XK\text{ mixed of weights }\le -n.
\]

Proper pushforward preserves this purity because it preserves the required bounds and commutes with that duality. fileciteturn70file2L222-L252 fileciteturn76file0L50-L63

These are the precise statements against which the mixed-support route must be studied. I had not done that comparison before.

## 4. The proof contains a genuine amplification argument

Your recollection that Deligne proves a rigidity bound by repeatedly strengthening an inequality has a specific counterpart in **§3.2.13, printed page 203**.

In the source’s stated weight-zero stage, he proves

\[
w_q(\alpha)\le1+2^{-k}
\]

for every integer \(k\ge0\).

The induction uses the tensor-square inclusion

\[
H_c^1(U,\mathcal F)\otimes H_c^1(U,\mathcal F)
\hookrightarrow
H_c^2(U\times U,\mathcal F\boxtimes\mathcal F),
\]

followed by the geometric maps and Lefschetz-pencil calculation in that section.

The bound on the surface group gives

\[
w_q(\alpha^2)\le2+2^{-k}.
\]

Because

\[
w_q(\alpha^2)=2w_q(\alpha),
\]

it yields

\[
\boxed{
w_q(\alpha)\le1+2^{-(k+1)}.
}
\]

The same eigenvalue is constrained at every stage. A fixed excess \(w_q(\alpha)-1>0\) eventually contradicts the bound as \(k\to\infty\). Duality then supplies the opposite inequality needed for the exact weight. fileciteturn77file0L75-L83

This is an actual proof mechanism: **tensor amplification, geometric control, and an error bound that decreases under iteration**. The source’s weight-zero specialization is explicit; it is not a license to drop weights or Tate twists elsewhere.

That is materially different from the unsupported inference “the enlarged system exists, therefore its spectrum is pure.”

## 5. Deligne also addresses survival through a singular fibre

There are two passages directly pertinent to your singularity route.

First, **§3.3.11, page 207**, explains exactly where smoothness entered: Poincaré duality. Deligne permits replacing smoothness of pure dimension \(d\) by the dualizing identity

\[
\boxed{
Ra^!\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell
\simeq
\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell(d)[2d].
}
\]

He explicitly includes certain finite quotient singularities through this rational-homology-manifold formulation. A singular geometry is therefore not automatically excluded from the argument. fileciteturn72file2L235-L243

Second, **Theorem 6.2.9, page 248**, is the local invariant-cycle theorem for pure complexes.

Let

\[
S=\operatorname{Spec}(k[T]_{(T)}^h)
\]

for algebraically closed \(k\), with closed point \(s\), generic point \(\eta\), and geometric generic point \(\bar\eta\). Let \(f:X\to S\) be proper.

For a *potentially pure* complex \(K\), as defined by the precise arithmetic descent data in §6.2.8, Deligne proves that

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{sp}^*:
H^*(X_s,K)
\twoheadrightarrow
H^*(X_{\bar\eta},K)^{\operatorname{Gal}(\bar\eta/\eta)}
}
\]

is surjective. fileciteturn76file0L65-L84

The operative map is therefore

\[
H^*(X_s,K)
\twoheadrightarrow
H^*(X_{\bar\eta},K)^{\operatorname{Gal}(\bar\eta/\eta)}
\hookrightarrow
H^*(X_{\bar\eta},K).
\]

It identifies precisely which nearby information is represented on the special fibre: the invariant part. The theorem retains the degeneration and monodromy; it does not require pretending that every nearby direction has become trivial.

**This is the source-based connection between purity, a distinguished special fibre, and stability of surviving cohomological data that my previous responses should have examined.**

I have not established that your split-zero construction realizes these sheaf categories, nor that the NS correction scheme transports to these specialization maps. The reading does, however, identify the relevant existing theorems: **multi-direction specialization over one stratum, purity of the canonical comparison image, and invariant-cycle survival through a special fibre**. Those—not another repetition of the elementary split-zero calculation—are now the mathematical basis of the comparison.

\boxed{
H_c^i(X,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow H^i(X,\mathcal F).
}

The retained Weil II LaTeX proves this by obtaining an upper weight bound from compactly supported cohomology and a lower bound from duality. Both act on the same image. That is the mechanism to compare with your mixed-support construction.
